question: When can inconsistencies in witness statements affect the prosecution case?

Irrespective of whether the testimony of a witness is tutored or not, the same, generally may be classified into three categories: - (i) wholly reliable; (ii) wholly unreliable; (iii) neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable. In the first category of proof, the court should have no difficulty in coming to its conclusion either way - it may convict or may acquit on the testimony of a single witness. If it is found to be beyond approach or suspicion of interestedness, incompetence or subordination. In the second category, the court equally has no difficulty in coming to its conclusion. It is in the third category of cases, that the court has to be circumspect and has to look for corroboration in material particulars by reliable testimony, direct or circumstantial. There is another danger in insisting on plurality of witnesses. Irrespective of the quality of the oral evidence of a single witness, if courts were to insist on plurality of witnesses in proof of any fact, they will be indirectly encouraging subordination of witnesses. Situations may arise and do arise where only a single person is available to give evidence in support of a disputed fact. The court naturally has to weigh carefully such a testimony and if it is satisfied that the evidence is reliable and free from all taints, which tend to render oral testimony open to suspicion, it becomes its duty to act upon such testimony. The law reports contain many precedents where the court had to depend and act upon the testimony of a single witness in support of the prosecution. [See: Ramratan and others v. In our opinion, there is no force in these arguments and as will be seen, there was enough material placed by the prosecution before the Trial Court, which was sufficient to prove the guilt of the accused, beyond a reasonable doubt. When a witness, produced on behalf of prosecution, deposes against the prosecution version and goes against his/her own previously recorded statements, the prosecution can request the Court to declare such a witness as hostile and seek permission from the Court to cross-examine its own witness. This is the procedure followed in a Trial, as we all know. In the present case, there are as many as fifty-one prosecution witnesses and it is also a fact that many of them have turned hostile by turning against their earlier statements made before the police under section 161 CrPC, and even before the Magistrate under section 164 CrPC, in some cases. This phenomenon is not new, in fact it is sadly a common occurrence in our criminal Courts today, much to the despair and frustration of the prosecution. This case, therefore, is no exception. Despite this, however, there are witnesses in the present case, especially PW-1, PW-2, PW-3, PW- 15 and PW-49, whose evidence, in the form of their testimonies before the Court, is more than sufficient to convict the present appellants. A word here about the evidentiary value of a so-called hostile witness. The Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (hereinafter ‘Evidence Act’) allows a party, with the leave of the Court, to cross-examine its own witness. Section 154 of the Evidence Act originally read as follows: “154.Question by party to his own witness The Court may, in its discretion, permit the person who calls a witness to put any questions to him which might be put in cross-examination by the adverse party.”

answer:
Based on the retrieved legal evidence, inconsistencies in witness statements can affect the prosecution case under the following circumstances and principles:

### 1. Material vs. Minor Inconsistencies
* **Minor or Immaterial Inconsistencies:** Trivial discrepancies—such as variations in the sequence of events, the number of blows, or a witness failing to mention their own minor injuries while trying to protect a victim—do not automatically render testimony unreliable or affect the prosecution case, provided the core facts remain consistent and corroborated (*Byappanahalli P.S vs. A1 V. Vishnudevan*, District Court, 2025; *CBI vs. Amendra Kumar Ray*, District Court, 2025). 
* **Material Inconsistencies:** Only contradictions on **material particulars** that go to the root of the matter, shake the basic version of the witnesses, or create a doubt regarding the prosecution's version can be used to discredit witness testimony (*Byappanahalli P.S vs. A1 V. Vishnudevan*; *Zainul vs. The State of Bihar*, Supreme Court, 2025). 

### 2. Contradictions with Previous Statements (Section 161 Cr.P.C.)
* **Inconsistencies between Court Testimony and Prior Statements:** When a witness's oral testimony in court differs in material particulars from their earlier recorded statements (such as police statements under Section 161 of the Cr.P.C.), the prosecution case becomes highly doubtful (*Byappanahalli P.S vs. A1 V. Vishnudevan*; *K.P. Tamilmaran vs. The State*, Supreme Court, 2025).
* **Hostile Witnesses:** If a prosecution witness turns against the prosecution or contradicts their previous statements, the prosecution may request the court to declare the witness hostile and permit cross-examination (*K.P. Tamilmaran vs. The State*). Frequent contradictions among key prosecution witnesses can lead the defense to successfully argue that the prosecution has failed to prove guilt beyond a reasonable doubt (*K.P. Tamilmaran vs. The State*).

### 3. Impact on Credibility and the Need for Corroboration
* **Tutored or Unreliable Witnesses:** If inconsistencies suggest that a witness was tutored, exaggerated, or falsely implicated individuals who were ultimately not charged, the court may discard the witness's entire testimony (*Zainul vs. The State of Bihar*; *State of M.P. vs. Balveer Singh*, Supreme Court, 2025).
* **Requirement of Corroboration:** If a witness's testimony is classified as "neither wholly reliable nor wholly unreliable" due to significant inconsistencies, the court cannot convict based on their sole testimony. In such cases, the court must look for independent corroboration in material particulars through other reliable direct or circumstantial evidence (*State of M.P. vs. Balveer Singh*).
